641: B is correct because enabling Cost and Usage Reports in the management account captures consolidated billing data for all member accounts, delivering the reports to Amazon S3 provides durable cheap storage, and Amazon Athena is a serverless query engine that runs standard SQL over the CUR files with no infrastructure to manage. Because the query runs only once a month, paying per query with Athena is far more cost-effective than running a persistent EMR cluster or streaming data into Kinesis. Additionally, reports only need to be enabled in the management account since it consolidates all member account usage.
642: A is correct because a Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and natively supports UDP traffic, which the gaming application requires. It also integrates with Auto Scaling groups so instances are automatically registered and deregistered as the group scales out and in. An Application Load Balancer only supports HTTP and HTTPS at Layer 7 and therefore cannot handle UDP packets.
643: A is correct because storing the logs in Amazon S3 is inexpensive and durable, and Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service that runs standard SQL directly against data in S3. Since the developers only analyze the logs on demand once a week, Athena's pay-per-query pricing model avoids the cost of running always-on infrastructure like an EMR cluster or OpenSearch domain. RDS is not suited for tens of gigabytes of unstructured log data per day.
644: A is correct because an ACM public certificate for the apex domain example.com along with a wildcard certificate for *.example.com covers the apex domain and all country subdomains, and public ACM certificates are the required type for terminating TLS on a public-facing Application Load Balancer. E is correct because validating domain ownership by adding the required CNAME DNS records to the DNS provider (DNS validation) allows ACM to automatically renew the certificates, keeping encryption in transit working without manual intervention. Private certificates are intended for internal use and would not work for a public website, and email validation does not support automatic renewal.
645: B is correct because an AWS KMS external key store (XKS) lets cryptographic keys remain outside of AWS in a third-party external key manager that the company controls, satisfying the regulatory requirement while still using AWS services for encryption and decryption. AWS manages the integration, supporting a variety of qualified external key managers from different vendors with the least operational overhead. CloudHSM options require the company to own and operate the key material inside an AWS-hosted HSM, which does not meet the requirement of retaining keys entirely outside the AWS Cloud.
646: C is correct because Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high-performance parallel file system designed for HPC workloads, providing sub-millisecond latency and high throughput to hundreds of EC2 instances accessing the same dataset simultaneously. Linking the FSx for Lustre file system to an S3 bucket lets engineers load the results into S3 for manual postprocessing after the distributed processing completes. Amazon EFS has higher per-operation latency that cannot reliably meet the 1 ms requirement, and S3 cannot be mounted as a POSIX shared file system.
647: A is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses served from the AWS global edge network, so user traffic is immediately directed to the closest healthy regional endpoint without any dependency on DNS resolution or IP address caching on user devices. Its continuous health checks automatically fail over traffic to another AWS Region if the primary endpoint becomes unavailable, meeting the global high-availability requirement. Route 53 geolocation routing is subject to DNS TTL caching on client devices, and CloudFront is optimized for HTTP content delivery rather than VoIP traffic.
648: B is correct because Amazon FSx for Lustre persistent file systems are highly available with redundant infrastructure and are built to deliver large amounts of sustained throughput to thousands of compute instances simultaneously, which matches the HPC requirement of sub-millisecond latency processing the entire dataset. Scratch file systems are temporary and not replicated, so they do not provide the required high availability. Amazon EFS offers higher per-operation latency and lower throughput levels than FSx for Lustre, in both bursting and provisioned throughput modes.
649: C is correct because the General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS volume type allows IOPS to be provisioned independently of storage capacity at a significantly lower cost per provisioned IOPS than io1 volumes. Provisioning 15,000 IOPS on gp3 meets the peak transaction requirement while minimizing cost. With gp2, IOPS scale with volume size so provisioning 15,000 IOPS would require a much larger and more expensive volume, and magnetic volumes cannot deliver that level of performance.
650: A is correct because Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server is a fully managed service that eliminates the OS patching, licensing, and database administration overhead of running SQL Server on EC2, while preserving compatibility with the existing SQL Server workload. RDS read replicas can be created for the data analysis team to run reporting queries without impacting the production transaction workload. The EC2 option requires the company to manage everything itself, and DynamoDB or Aurora MySQL would require rewriting the application to change database engines.
651: C is correct because S3 Standard-IA after 180 days provides a lower-cost tier for infrequently accessed data while still storing it redundantly across multiple Availability Zones, satisfying the requirement that no data can be lost. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 360 days meets the archival requirement with millisecond retrieval so archived images remain instantly available on request. S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 years is the lowest-cost storage class and its standard retrieval completes within 12 hours, matching the auditors' retrieval requirement. One Zone-IA stores data in only a single Availability Zone, which risks data loss and does not meet the durability requirement.
652: B is correct because a transient EMR cluster automatically terminates after the 6-hour daily job finishes, so the company only pays for compute during actual processing, which is the most cost-effective approach for a daily batch workload. Running the primary node and core nodes (which store HDFS data) on On-Demand Instances protects the master services and data against Spot interruption so no data is lost during the run. Task nodes can safely run on Spot Instances because they are stateless and add capacity without holding critical HDFS data.
653: B is correct because an AWS Lambda function can look up the creating user's cost center from the RDS database and apply the correct cost center tag to the resource, giving each resource a dynamic tag based on who created it. An Amazon EventBridge rule that reacts to AWS CloudTrail events can invoke the Lambda function in near real time whenever a resource creation event occurs in the specific AWS account. A scheduled rule would run periodically rather than on each creation event, and tagging with a default value does not capture the actual user's cost center.
654: D is correct because Amazon CloudFront with an S3 origin is a managed, highly available way to deliver static content globally, while an Application Load Balancer targeting an ECS service running Fargate tasks provides a managed, highly available compute platform for the PHP application. ElastiCache for Redis running across multiple Availability Zones replaces the local Redis server with a fault-tolerant managed session store shared by all application tasks. Every component is an AWS managed service, and no single EC2 instance remains a single point of failure.
655: C is correct because a public Application Load Balancer provides an internet-facing endpoint that integrates with the existing target group and supports session affinity (sticky sessions), which is a Layer 7 feature unavailable on Network and Gateway Load Balancers. E is correct because creating a web ACL in AWS WAF and associating it with the ALB endpoint applies managed and custom rule protections to inspect and filter incoming HTTP traffic for additional security. Network Load Balancers operate at Layer 4 and do not support sticky sessions or native AWS WAF association.
656: D is correct because S3 Standard-IA is significantly cheaper than S3 Standard for objects that are accessed only once or twice a year, while still storing data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones for high availability, and S3 static website hosting can deliver the images directly without any servers to manage. Standard-IA retrieval fees are negligible given the extremely low access frequency, making it the most cost-effective highly available option. EBS and EFS both require EC2 web servers whose costs are unjustified for rarely accessed images, and S3 Standard costs more for this access pattern.
657: B is correct because a customer managed prefix list stores the office CIDR ranges in one place, and sharing it with AWS Resource Access Manager makes the single prefix list available to all accounts in the organization. Security groups across the organization reference the prefix list, so when a CIDR range is added or removed, the update to the prefix list automatically propagates to every security group that uses it, eliminating the need to edit rules account by account. This centralized, serverless approach requires no Lambda functions, Firewall Manager policies, or cross-account security group management, making it the most cost-effective solution.
658: A is correct because deploying the compute optimized EC2 instances into a cluster placement group places them in the same Availability Zone with low-latency, high-bandwidth networking, which minimizes latency for the HPC workloads. E is correct because Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the only listed file system that provides multi-protocol NFS and SMB access from a single file system, replicating the on-premises NAS capability in the cloud. FSx for Lustre and FSx for OpenZFS do not support both NFS and SMB protocols simultaneously.
659: C is correct because AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized can physically transport up to about 80 TB of usable storage, easily handling the 50 TB of data securely with encryption, and the transfer is not dependent on network bandwidth. The existing Site-to-Site VPN is already 90 percent utilized, so pushing 50 TB over it within 2 weeks is not feasible, and a Direct Connect link takes weeks to provision and is a poor fit for a one-time transfer.
660: D is correct because a scheduled scaling policy tells the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances at a set time before the known peak hours begin, so capacity is already in place when traffic arrives and the application performs properly at the start of peak hours. The current slowness is caused by reactive scaling being too slow to respond at the beginning of the predictable peak. Dynamic scaling policies based on CPU or memory only add capacity after utilization has already spiked, and a load balancer does not add capacity.
